name: Protagoras's practical defense of convention despite scepticism
plain_explanation: Even though Protagoras said he could not be sure whether the gods exist, he still thought people ought to worship them, and he generally supported following established laws and customs.
precise_definition: Protagoras's position that, since there is no objective truth to appeal to, the majority becomes for practical purposes the arbiter of belief, which led him to defend law, convention, and traditional morality, including worship of gods whose existence he professed himself unable to affirm or deny.
why_it_mattered: Russell presents this as 'the right' position for a thoroughgoing and logical theoretical sceptic to hold, since without an objective standard, practical and social convention is the only available guide to action.
examples: Protagoras's opening line from On the Gods: 'With regard to the gods, I cannot feel sure either that they are or that they are not...'
competing_positions: Thrasymachus's and Callicles's more radical position, that justice/law is merely the interest of the stronger, which Russell explicitly says is not characteristic of the Sophists generally
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly reconciles theoretical scepticism about the gods with practical religious and social conservatism.
